title: Classification (Publications, Films and Computer Games) Amendment (Classification Tools and Other Measures) Bill 2014
short_title: Classification (Publications, Films and Computer Games) Amendment (Classification Tools and Other Measures) Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would update Australia's national classification system for publications, films and computer games based on initial recommendations from a law reform review.

It would allow automated classification tools, require classification markings on all rated content, and let the Attorney-General's Department alert police about potentially refused-classification material without a prior decision.

The bill also makes minor amendments, including giving the minister explicit power to set rules for displaying consumer advice and replacing the requirement for Senior Classifiers with a discretion to appoint them.
changes: Expands exemptions for films shown at festivals and cultural institutions.
Permits classification via automated tools like online questionnaires.
Makes classification markings mandatory on all classified content.
Broadens exceptions so modified films and games do not need re-classification.
Lets the Attorney-General's Department notify law enforcement of potential refused-classification content before formal classification.
Gives the minister power to determine consumer advice display rules.
summary.affected: Consumers, film and computer game distributors, festivals, cultural institutions, the Classification Board, the Attorney-General's Department, and law enforcement authorities.

speeches.speaker: David Feeney
speeches.brief: Supported the Classification Amendment Bill's first tranche of reforms, recounted that the Australian Law Reform Commission's 2012 report made 57 recommendations following a review the former Labor government commissioned, and said the bill implements six of those recommendations while broadening exemptions and streamlining reclassification requirements for modified content.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Laming
speeches.brief: Argued that the classification reforms are simple changes that Labor failed to make in 6½ years of government, welcomed streamlined exemptions for modified games and films needing reclassification, and said the updated system, developed 20 years after the original 1995 scheme, will benefit gamers and parents in Bowman.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: Supported the Classification Amendment Bill, recounted the 2011 Australian Law Reform Commission review that drew almost 1,500 submissions and produced a 400-page report with 57 recommendations, and welcomed the new International Age Rating Coalition tool to speed up a process that assessed over 6,000 applications last year.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: Thanked members for their contributions on the Classification Amendment Bill, noted Labor was in government from 2007 to 2013 without implementing this reform, and said the bill's first tranche was agreed by state and territory classification ministers at the Standing Council on Law and Justice meeting in April 2013.

speeches.speaker: Laurie Ferguson
speeches.brief: Presented a report examining 22 bills and 42 legislative instruments for compatibility with human rights. Raised concerns that national uniform schemes negotiated through COAG can be agreed without formal human rights scrutiny, and sought an update on efforts to address this in drafting protocols for national legislation.
